options: The machine Docker runs on — your laptop or a server — where containers run
primer-core-concepts.why: The host is the computer running Docker. Containers run 'on the host', and 'localhost' from your shell means this machine.

options: A generic term for one machine in a group; in Docker, a machine running containers
primer-core-concepts.why: A node is one machine among several. You'll use the word constantly in Kubernetes; in Docker it just means a machine that runs containers.

primer-core-concepts.q: Why are containers lighter than virtual machines, in kernel terms?
options: Containers share the host's kernel; VMs each ship their own full operating system
Containers run without any operating system at all
primer-core-concepts.why: A VM virtualizes hardware and runs a whole OS (heavy). A container shares the host's Linux kernel, so it's just isolated processes — light and fast.

primer-core-concepts.q: Inside a container, what does 'localhost' refer to?
options: The container itself — not your laptop or another container
primer-core-concepts.why: Each container has its own network identity, so 'localhost' inside it means that container. To reach another container, use its name on a shared network.

options: Image = read-only blueprint; container = a running instance of an image; 'instance' = one running copy of something
They are three words for the same file
An image runs; a container is stored
An instance is a type of registry
primer-core-concepts.why: You build an image once and start many containers (instances) from it — like baking many cookies from one cutter.

options: Docker's modern build engine — parallel stages, better caching, build secrets, and multi-platform output; the default builder
08-buildkit-buildx-multiplatform.why: BuildKit is the backend behind docker build (default in current Docker), exposed via buildx. It's faster and far more capable than the old builder.

options: amd64 and arm64 are incompatible; a multi-arch image runs on both, so you publish once and run anywhere
Because Docker requires two images per app
08-buildkit-buildx-multiplatform.why: An image built for one CPU architecture won't run on the other. A multi-arch image bundles both, and the runtime pulls the right one.

08-buildkit-buildx-multiplatform.q: Why do multi-platform builds usually go straight to a registry with --push?
options: The local image store holds one architecture at a time; the registry stores the multi-arch manifest
Registries build the image for you
08-buildkit-buildx-multiplatform.why: A single local Docker image is one architecture. The multi-arch manifest (linking both) lives in a registry, so you push it directly.

08-buildkit-buildx-multiplatform.q: How do you use a credential at build time without leaking it into the image?
options: RUN --mount=type=secret with --secret — available for that RUN only, never stored in a layer
Put it in an ENV instruction
COPY the secret file into the image
08-buildkit-buildx-multiplatform.why: BuildKit build secrets are mounted just for one RUN and never written to a layer, so 'docker history' won't reveal them — unlike ENV/COPY.

options: Persists a directory (e.g. the package cache) across builds so dependencies aren't re-downloaded each time
08-buildkit-buildx-multiplatform.why: A cache mount keeps something like the npm/apt cache between builds, so even when the layer rebuilds, deps aren't fetched again — big CI speedups.

11-challenges-projects.q: Why do build-from-a-spec challenges build skill that guided labs alone don't?
options: You build from a spec without step-by-step guidance — the way real work and interviews test you
11-challenges-projects.why: Following steps builds recognition; producing a working result from requirements builds the transferable competence jobs actually test.

11-challenges-projects.q: In the multi-stage challenge, what made the image tiny?
options: A multi-stage build shipping only the final binary on a slim base — no build tools
Deleting the source after building in the same image
11-challenges-projects.why: The build stage compiles; a clean runtime stage copies only the artifact. Build tools and source never ship, so the image is a few MB.

11-challenges-projects.q: In the Compose stack challenge, what gave the database persistence and readiness?
options: A named volume for its data and a healthcheck reporting healthy
Publishing its port to the host
11-challenges-projects.why: A named volume keeps the data across container recreation; a healthcheck lets Compose report the DB as truly ready, not just started.

11-challenges-projects.q: In the persistence challenge, why did the data survive destroying the container?
options: It lived in a named volume mounted into the replacement container, not in the container's writable layer
The data was stored in the image
11-challenges-projects.why: Mounting the same named volume into the new container reattaches the data, which lives independently of any single container.

11-challenges-projects.q: In the capstone, what does a multi-arch image let you do?
options: Publish one tag that runs on both amd64 and arm64 — publish once, run anywhere
11-challenges-projects.why: A multi-architecture image serves the correct build to each platform automatically, so the same tag works on Intel and ARM machines.

setup-local-docker.q: What single application do you install to use Docker locally?
setup-local-docker.why: Docker Desktop bundles the engine and tools on Mac/Windows; on Linux you install Docker Engine directly. That's all you need.

setup-local-docker.q: What did 'docker run hello-world' actually do?
options: Pulled an image from a registry, created a container from it, and ran it
setup-local-docker.why: It demonstrated the whole pipeline: fetch image → create container → run. --rm then cleaned the container up.

options: Publish the container's port 80 to your machine's port 8080
setup-local-docker.why: -p HOST:CONTAINER maps a host port to a container port so you can reach the containerized service from your machine.

setup-local-docker.q: How do you get a shell inside a running container?
setup-local-docker.why: exec runs a new command in an already-running container; -it makes it interactive so you get a usable shell.

setup-local-docker.q: Which two commands stop and then remove a container?
setup-local-docker.why: stop halts the container gracefully; rm removes the stopped container. (docker rm -f does both at once.)

options: They package an app with everything it needs so it runs the same everywhere
They make code run faster on the CPU
They replace the need for a programming language
They store backups of your data
primer-what-are-containers.why: By bundling app + runtime + libraries + settings, a container behaves identically on any machine — ending 'works on my machine.'

primer-what-are-containers.q: What is the key difference between a container and a virtual machine?
options: A VM ships a whole guest OS (heavy); a container shares the host OS kernel (light, fast)
A container ships a whole OS; a VM shares the kernel
A container needs special hardware; a VM doesn't
primer-what-are-containers.why: VMs virtualize hardware and run full OSes (GBs, slow boot). Containers virtualize the OS, sharing the kernel — MBs, millisecond start.

primer-what-are-containers.q: What is the difference between an image and a container?
options: An image is the read-only blueprint; a container is a running instance of it
An image runs; a container is just a file
primer-what-are-containers.why: Image = recipe/blueprint (doesn't run). Container = the blueprint brought to life. One image can spawn many containers.

primer-what-are-containers.q: Can you run many containers from one image?
options: No — each image runs exactly one container
Only if the image is small
primer-what-are-containers.why: Like baking many cookies from one cutter, you can start any number of containers from a single image.

primer-what-are-containers.q: What is Docker, in one line?
options: The most popular tool for building images and running containers
primer-what-are-containers.why: Docker gives simple commands (build, run) and the image format the industry standardized on.

00-what-is-docker.q: What are the three stages of the Docker lifecycle?
options: Build an image, ship it to a registry, run it as containers
00-what-is-docker.why: Build (Dockerfile → image), Ship (push to a registry), Run (start containers). Kubernetes scales up the 'run' stage.

00-what-is-docker.q: What's the difference between the Docker CLI and the daemon?
options: The CLI is what you type; the daemon is the background engine that builds/runs and holds images
The CLI runs containers; the daemon is just for logging
The daemon is the command you type
00-what-is-docker.why: You type `docker` (CLI), which sends requests over an API to the daemon (dockerd), which does the actual work.

00-what-is-docker.q: Why do Docker images run on Kubernetes and other runtimes?
options: They follow the open OCI standard, so any OCI-compatible runtime can run them
Kubernetes secretly installs Docker on every node
Images are rewritten for each platform
They don't — you must rebuild for Kubernetes
00-what-is-docker.why: The image format and runtime are OCI standards, so images built with Docker run on containerd, CRI-O, Podman, and Kubernetes unchanged.

00-what-is-docker.q: Docker vs Kubernetes, in one line each?
options: Docker builds/runs containers on a machine; Kubernetes orchestrates many containers across many machines
Docker is for Windows; Kubernetes is for Linux
They are competing products that do the same thing
Kubernetes builds images; Docker runs them
00-what-is-docker.why: You build with Docker and operate at scale with Kubernetes, which runs the very images Docker builds.

00-what-is-docker.q: What file is the recipe for building an image?
00-what-is-docker.why: docker build runs the instructions in a Dockerfile top-to-bottom to produce an image.

01-images-and-layers.q: What is a layer in a Docker image?
options: A read-only set of filesystem changes; build instructions stack into layers that combine into the image
A backup copy of the image
01-images-and-layers.why: Each instruction records only what changed, as a layer. Stacked via a union filesystem, they present as one image.

options: Shared/cached storage between images and fast rebuilds via layer caching
They make containers run as root
They remove the need for a registry
01-images-and-layers.why: Common base layers are stored once and shared; unchanged layers are reused on rebuild, so builds and pulls are fast.

01-images-and-layers.q: Does the tag 'latest' mean 'the newest version'?
options: No — it's just a default tag; pin a real version in production
Yes — Docker always resolves it to the newest release
Yes, but only for official images
It means the image is broken
01-images-and-layers.why: 'latest' is whatever was last pushed under that tag — not magically newest. Production should pin explicit version tags.

options: A tag is a movable human label; a digest is an immutable content hash of an exact image
A digest is a nickname; a tag is a hash
A tag is for private images; a digest for public ones
01-images-and-layers.why: Tags can be repointed; a @sha256 digest always identifies the exact same image — ideal for reproducible deploys.

01-images-and-layers.q: What happens to an image's layers when a container writes files?
options: The image stays read-only; the container gets a thin writable layer on top
The image's layers are modified in place
The write fails — containers can't write
A new image is automatically pushed
01-images-and-layers.why: Images are read-only. A running container adds a throwaway writable layer, which is why its changes vanish when it's removed.

02-lab-run-manage-containers.q: What's the difference between 'docker run' and 'docker exec'?
options: run creates a new container from an image; exec runs a command in an already-running container
run is for images; exec is for volumes
exec creates containers; run inspects them
02-lab-run-manage-containers.why: Use run to start a fresh container; use exec to execute something inside a container that's already up (e.g. a debug shell).

02-lab-run-manage-containers.q: What does '-d' do, and when do you want it?
02-lab-run-manage-containers.why: -d runs the container in the background and returns your prompt — right for servers you want to keep running.

02-lab-run-manage-containers.q: Your first two debugging commands when a container misbehaves?
02-lab-run-manage-containers.why: logs shows what the app said; inspect shows its full config, mounts, env, and last state. Start there.

02-lab-run-manage-containers.q: Why did an in-container file edit survive 'start' but not 'rm'?
options: It lived in the container's writable layer; removing the container deletes that layer
Docker only saves edits on Tuesdays
The edit was written to the image
start rebuilds the container from scratch
02-lab-run-manage-containers.why: stop/start keep the same container (and its writable layer). rm destroys the container and its layer — so persist data in volumes.

options: Removes unused Docker data — stopped containers, dangling images, etc. — to reclaim disk
Deletes all your images including in-use ones with no warning
Publishes your images to a registry
02-lab-run-manage-containers.why: It reclaims space by removing unused resources (it prompts first). Handy when Docker's disk usage grows.

03-dockerfiles.q: What does each instruction in a Dockerfile roughly produce?
options: A layer; docker build runs the instructions top to bottom
03-dockerfiles.why: Instructions like FROM/RUN/COPY each add a layer. The build executes them in order to assemble the image.

03-dockerfiles.q: Why copy package.json and install dependencies BEFORE copying the source?
options: So the cached dependency layer is reused unless deps change; source edits don't trigger a reinstall
03-dockerfiles.why: Layer caching: put least-changing steps first. Dependencies rarely change, so that expensive install layer stays cached across code edits.

options: CMD is an easily-overridden default command; ENTRYPOINT is a fixed executable that takes run-time args as its arguments
ENTRYPOINT is overridden by default; CMD is fixed
CMD runs at build time; ENTRYPOINT at run time
03-dockerfiles.why: docker run myapp <x> overrides CMD entirely, but is passed as arguments to an ENTRYPOINT. Use ENTRYPOINT when the image *is* a command.

options: Excluding files from the build context — faster builds and no leaked secrets/junk
Telling Kubernetes which pods to skip
03-dockerfiles.why: It keeps things like node_modules, .git, and .env out of the build context, speeding builds and preventing secret leaks into images.

03-dockerfiles.q: What does '-t' do in 'docker build -t name:tag .'?
options: Names and tags the resulting image; '.' is the build context
Runs the build in a terminal
03-dockerfiles.why: -t assigns a repository:tag to the built image so you can refer to it; the trailing path is the build context sent to the daemon.

04-data-volumes.q: Why can't important data live in the container itself?
options: The writable layer is deleted when the container is removed — containers are ephemeral
The data is sent to the registry
04-data-volumes.why: A container's changes live in its throwaway writable layer. Removing the container deletes them, so persistent data must live outside.

04-data-volumes.q: Named volume versus bind mount — the core difference?
options: A volume is Docker-managed storage referenced by name; a bind mount maps a specific host folder
A volume maps a host folder; a bind mount is Docker-managed
A volume is read-only; a bind mount is read-write
04-data-volumes.why: Volumes are managed by Docker and portable; bind mounts point at an exact directory on your machine.

04-data-volumes.q: Which storage type do you use for a production database?
04-data-volumes.why: Named volumes are Docker-managed, portable, and survive container removal — the recommended home for app data like databases.

04-data-volumes.q: Which storage type is ideal for live-editing code during development?
04-data-volumes.why: A bind mount maps your source folder into the container so edits appear instantly — no rebuild needed.

04-data-volumes.q: What does ':ro' do on a mount?
options: Makes it read-only inside the container
Marks it as a root-owned mount
04-data-volumes.why: ro = read-only; the container can read the mounted data but not modify it. Drop it for read-write.

options: Publishes container port 80 to host port 8080 so you can reach it
Limits the container to 80 MB of memory
05-networking.why: Publishing maps a host port to a container port so traffic from your machine reaches the containerized service.

05-networking.q: On a user-defined bridge network, how do containers find each other?
options: By container name — Docker provides automatic DNS
05-networking.why: User-defined bridge networks include DNS, so a container can reach another by its name (e.g. connect to 'db').

05-networking.q: Why create a user-defined network instead of using the default bridge?
options: Automatic name-based DNS between containers; the default bridge lacks it
The default bridge can't reach the internet
05-networking.why: Name resolution between containers only works on user-defined networks, which is why multi-container apps should use one.

05-networking.q: Does a container need '-p' to reach the internet?
options: No — outbound works by default; -p is only for inbound access
05-networking.why: Containers can make outbound connections via NAT out of the box. Publishing (-p) is only needed to accept inbound traffic.

05-networking.q: Should a database container usually publish its port?
options: No — only the app needs it over the private network; publishing exposes it unnecessarily
05-networking.why: If only your app talks to the DB, keep it on the private network unpublished. Publishing exposes the database to your whole host/LAN.

06-docker-compose.q: What does 'docker compose up' do that saves you effort?
options: Starts all services and auto-creates their network and volumes — no long docker run commands
06-docker-compose.why: Compose reads the whole stack from one YAML file and brings it up together, wiring networking and volumes automatically.

06-docker-compose.q: How does the 'api' service reach the database in Compose?
options: By the service name 'db' as a hostname on the auto-created network
By the database's IP address hard-coded in the app
06-docker-compose.why: Compose puts services on a shared network with DNS; the service name doubles as its hostname (e.g. db:5432).

06-docker-compose.q: What does 'depends_on' guarantee — and not guarantee?
options: Start order; not that the dependency is actually ready — use healthchecks for readiness
06-docker-compose.why: depends_on sequences container startup but doesn't wait for the app inside to be ready. Add healthchecks for true readiness.

06-docker-compose.q: What's the danger of 'docker compose down -v'?
options: The -v deletes named volumes — you lose the data
It rebuilds all images from scratch
06-docker-compose.why: Plain 'down' removes containers and the network; adding -v also removes named volumes, permanently deleting persisted data.

06-docker-compose.q: Why is Compose good preparation for Kubernetes?
options: It's declarative — you describe the desired stack and Compose makes it so, the mindset Kubernetes uses
It runs across many machines like Kubernetes
It replaces the need to learn Kubernetes
06-docker-compose.why: Compose introduces declarative, multi-service thinking. Kubernetes uses the same mindset at cluster scale with more power.

07-image-optimization-security.q: What does a multi-stage build achieve?
options: Builds in one stage and ships only the final artifact in a clean stage — much smaller, no build tools
Runs the build twice for safety
Splits the app across multiple containers
07-image-optimization-security.why: A build stage compiles; a slim runtime stage copies only the output. Build tools and source never ship — often 80–95% smaller.

07-image-optimization-security.q: Why delete apt caches in the SAME RUN layer where you install?
options: Deleting in a later layer doesn't shrink the image; the earlier layer still contains the files
It has no effect either way
07-image-optimization-security.why: Each layer is immutable. Files added in one layer persist even if removed in a later one, so clean up within the same RUN.

07-image-optimization-security.q: Why should you never put secrets in a Dockerfile or ENV?
options: They're baked into layers permanently and visible via docker history; pass secrets at run time
It makes the image smaller but insecure
07-image-optimization-security.why: Anything in the image (including build-time ENV) is inspectable forever. Provide secrets at run time via env, mounts, or a secret manager.

07-image-optimization-security.q: Why avoid running a container as root?
options: A container breakout would be root on the host; run as a non-root user
Root containers can't reach the network
Root is not allowed by Docker
07-image-optimization-security.why: Containers run as root by default; adding a USER limits the blast radius if the container is compromised.

07-image-optimization-security.q: One command to check an image for known vulnerabilities?
07-image-optimization-security.why: docker scout cves reports known CVEs in an image's packages. Smaller images with fewer packages typically have far fewer.

options: A shared store for images that you push to and others/servers/Kubernetes pull from
A log of every container that has run
09-registries-distribution.why: Registries (Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, etc.) host named, tagged images so they can travel from your laptop to servers and clusters.

options: registry ghcr.io, namespace acme, repository api, tag 1.4.2
namespace ghcr.io, registry acme, tag api, repo 1.4.2
It's all just the repository name
09-registries-distribution.why: Fully-qualified names are registry/namespace/repository:tag. Missing parts default to docker.io and :latest.

options: No — it adds another name pointing at the same layers
09-registries-distribution.why: Tagging just creates an additional reference to the same image content; push then uploads only layers the registry lacks.

options: It's ambiguous and makes rollbacks/debugging hard; deploy specific version tags
latest can't be pulled by servers
09-registries-distribution.why: 'latest' can point at different content over time, so you can't reliably know or roll back what's deployed. Pin explicit versions.

options: No — it pulls prebuilt images from a registry and runs them
Yes — it builds from your Dockerfile on each node
09-registries-distribution.why: Kubernetes runs images; it doesn't build them. Your CI builds and pushes images, and Kubernetes pulls them by name.

10-debugging-production.q: What does a HEALTHCHECK add over 'the container is running'?
options: It tests the app itself, so Docker knows healthy vs unhealthy — the basis of Kubernetes probes
10-debugging-production.why: A process can be 'running' but broken. A healthcheck probes the app so orchestrators can restart or route around it.

10-debugging-production.q: Which restart policy suits a long-running service?
10-debugging-production.why: unless-stopped restarts the container across crashes and reboots, but respects a manual stop. 'always' is similar but ignores manual stops.

10-debugging-production.q: Where should containerized apps write their logs?
options: To stdout/stderr — the platform captures and ships them
To a file inside the container
10-debugging-production.why: Logging to stdout/stderr lets Docker capture output (docker logs) and lets logging drivers/Kubernetes ship it centrally.

10-debugging-production.q: A container exits immediately. What's the first command to run?
options: docker logs <c> — the crash reason is usually there (and docker ps -a shows the exit code)
10-debugging-production.why: Logs almost always contain the error. ps -a shows the exit code (e.g. 1 = app error, 137 = OOM-killed).

10-debugging-production.q: What does exit code 137 usually mean?
options: OOM-killed / SIGKILL — often a memory limit was exceeded
10-debugging-production.why: 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL). It commonly means the container hit its memory limit and was killed.

12-next-steps-kubernetes.q: What's the fundamental limit of Docker/Compose that Kubernetes removes?
options: They run on one machine; Kubernetes orchestrates containers across a cluster of machines
12-next-steps-kubernetes.why: Docker/Compose are single-host. Kubernetes schedules, scales, and self-heals containers across many machines.

12-next-steps-kubernetes.q: What Kubernetes object corresponds to a running container?
options: A Pod (one or more containers, the smallest unit)
12-next-steps-kubernetes.why: A Pod wraps one (or a few tightly-coupled) containers and is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes.

12-next-steps-kubernetes.q: What replaces 'docker run' for declaring desired, self-healing replicas?
12-next-steps-kubernetes.why: A Deployment declares how many replicas of an image you want and continuously keeps that many healthy, handling rollouts.

12-next-steps-kubernetes.q: What does a Kubernetes Service provide that '-p' did locally?
options: A stable name plus load balancing across many pods
12-next-steps-kubernetes.why: A Service gives a durable name/IP and spreads traffic across all matching pods, however many there are and wherever they run.

12-next-steps-kubernetes.q: Name the core mindset shift going from Docker to Kubernetes.
options: Imperative → declarative: describe desired state and let the system maintain it
Declarative → imperative: run each command by hand
From containers back to virtual machines
12-next-steps-kubernetes.why: Instead of 'run this container,' you declare 'keep 5 healthy replicas' and Kubernetes continuously reconciles reality to match.

13-runtime-security-limits.q: Why is running the container process as root a real risk, even though it's 'root inside a namespace'?
options: A container-escape bug turns namespace-root into host-root; a non-root user denies that outcome
Docker refuses to start root containers in production
13-runtime-security-limits.why: Isolation is a default, not a guarantee. If an escape bug lands, the attacker holds whatever identity the process had — USER appuser means an escape lands as an unprivileged user, not the host's root.
whyWrong: Performance is identical; privilege is the issue.
Docker happily runs root containers — that's the default, which is the problem.
Health checks don't care about the user at all.

13-runtime-security-limits.q: A container keeps dying with exit code 137, while another is mysteriously slow with healthy dependencies. What's happening?
options: 137 is the memory limit killing the container (OOMKilled); the slow one is being CPU-throttled — memory limits kill, CPU limits throttle
Exit 137 means a Dockerfile syntax error
13-runtime-security-limits.why: The two limits fail differently, and the difference is the diagnostic: hitting the memory cap is fatal (SIGKILL, 137), hitting the CPU cap just slows the process down. docker stats and docker inspect confirm which.
whyWrong: CPU limits never kill a container — they only throttle it.
Neither symptom points at the network; both are cgroup behaviors.
137 is 128+9: killed by SIGKILL — a runtime event, not a build error.

13-runtime-security-limits.q: A README tells you to run the container with --privileged. What should you conclude?
options: It's fine — privileged mode is just faster
The software needs the whole host: --privileged disables essentially all isolation, and a narrower flag (--cap-add, --device) is almost always the honest alternative
It's required for containers that use volumes
13-runtime-security-limits.why: --privileged grants every capability, every device, and drops seccomp — the container effectively IS the host. Legitimate needs are nearly always one capability or one device; grant exactly that instead.
whyWrong: It affects far more than networking — devices, capabilities, syscall filtering, everything.
Volumes work fine in ordinary containers; no privilege needed.
